en: He did not sit still without struggling,
He became a dear khan over China,
He became the head of the hostile force,
He devastated the Kyrgyz people.
These Kyrgyz are beyond the wind’s reach.
They have ruined your undertaking,
And struck your strength from your waist.
They have laid you in your grave.
Brave Orozan, lord of Chokon’s people,
They have undone the people you set in order.
There is no man left; they have grown numerous.
The enemy behind you has become few.
My strength that had girded itself,
My manly guardian, hold firm.
You will come into this world,
To the resounding shield,
You are a keen and deadly marksman.
You were a wrestler and a champion.
You alone were the one I trusted.
Even if the earth fell before you,
The wind could not overtake you in battle.
Come after binding the people’s hands.
Gouge out both their eyes,
Cut out their tongues without dragging them,
And slash them from the nape.
Exact the Kalmyk’s grief by force.
Kick him in the ribs,
Mount him upon the iron,
Drive him on in humiliation,
Shove him away and burn him,
And drive him here before me.
You were a brave man and a champion.
The broad son of the Burut,
The towering Sungai falcon,
The broad one from Kök-Chalkan,
Your champion who rode out to the contest—
Do not make the road of his horse a drove-road,
His neck was vast as Ala-Too.
He appeared like a shield for the people,
He drained the strength of the multitude,
His arm was a block, his heart stone,
His eloquent tongue stirred great tumult,
Taking position like a variegated army,
So many of the white-capped people,
The condition of hero Kenen,
Find his people and hold them.
Passed down from the storytellers,
Asked of countless youths,
With the swift and famed marksman,
Wading through the surging blood,
Caught in distress,
Koyka Bash, who had become Kyrgyz,
The sword passed and severed his spine,
Hero Üytkör kept his eyes open,
He lost his fierce strength,
At the time he left the battle,
It was a mountain he would climb untired,
He was a warrior who advanced without stopping,
His fur-capped eyes blazed,
No one had another youth like him,
My falcon of the mountains,
He would plunge into bloody battle,
Never retreating from it,
He would lie down with his saddlecloth,
His weary eyes could no longer see,
May the shattered spear not strike,
Kenen watched and was delayed,
Like an unyielding warrior,
He descended without abandoning his stance,
Köböy swayed among them all,
May the living Kyrgyz not abandon him,
Such was the warrior’s lionheartedness.
All that has come down from the forefathers,
He knew with stern attention.
That dark Kyrgyz still rides on.
Upon Beijing’s golden throne,
Where its people were established in splendor,
Saying China would suffer calamity from the Burut,
Saying any man who grappled with him would die.
From the Kyrgyz farther beyond,
It was inscribed under a vanished rule.
Saying, “I shall take the Burut,”
When they heard this news,
The khans rode out from Kaken.
The lion never turned back.
Of the Burut who joined the battle,
From his harsh and grievous lament,
He pondered deeply and took a horse.
The people of Beijing once again,
The dark warrior Kozhojan,
A marksman like you rode out.
Not one soul turned back.
They prepared for the great ordeal,
For the grave face of hardship.
He entered it on that register.
Understand what we have said.
Behind you stood only the marksman.
My strength was no mere child.
You were a champion and a hero.
You were the lamb that turned the flock.
You were the gray-maned hero himself.
No bullet pierced what he wore.
No mane could overtake what he rode.
Those who heard the name Burut,
If the champion committed his people,
The stratagems of mighty Beijing,
The champion would spill blood like embers.
You were livestock standing at the stake.
From your elder came Kördün,
For that cause they gave their lives,
Saying, “Consider these words of mine,”
He said this to the marksman,
He spoke of your stern countenance,
The lord spoke to Kenen,
Not knowing your brave warrior,
To the khan of Alboo,
Chongteñir showed his might,
Before champion Üytkör’s company,
Üytkör remained at death’s threshold,
As he watched his spoils,
Saying they swept through without bending,
Saying he departed into the depths,
Saying, “I reached straight from the foundation,”
Calling the massed Chinese a surging flood,
Saying, “Take the risk and strike straight,”
Like an iron rope drawn taut,
Heavenly Khan beneath earth and sky,
The two hands of battle were joined,
Without halting his hand, he pressed the deed,
The marksman recognized the hero,
He knew the brave man would face him,
How poor his strength had become,
Hero Kenen kept watch,
He struck like a worthy man,
They handed the brave man to the punishing host.
Standing enraged,
From the black earth the war drum sounded,
The wrathful lord struck hard,
The beast remained without regaining sense,
He trod the mist-covered ground,
Shattering stone and gouging the mountain,
Crossing water without tiring,
Ozu Khan seized the great battlefield.
Whichever side he watched from,
Seeing the Chinese host,
They thrust their spears without tiring,
They stood beneath the banner,
Blood sprayed as he was left exposed,
They did not fear the gathered host,
When the declining day struck,
Across the yellow plain bright as the moon,
They soaked it in abundant red blood,
His body stood like a ravine fortress,
Warriors who shattered the Chinese,
When the champion attacked from the front,
He met the banner he had charged,
Jeljetpes of middle stature,
It was the time he reached his place,
Hero Kenen stood in the very center,
It was the time they were draining his strength,
At the far edge stood two heroes,
It was the time they drove them on,
May the one who drove them be damned,
Of the Chinese grave-bound host,
Overwhelmed by immeasurable numbers,
God delivered them to calamity,
The Kyrgyz spring against China,
The spring mouth turned back,
The Kyrgyz were alone; the Chinese countless,
Köböy wrote it into history,
He set nine against one,
He left its history upon Talas,
Ninety men against one soul,
When he struck, he left them alone,
No person escapes tribulation,
Kertulpar beneath you,
A creature of fierce disposition.
If the browed maral did not yield,
If his steadfast soul found no rest,
If his livestock did not tire on the rough ground,
If not a handful of my order remained,
If they tested him, saying, “Enter the wrestling,”
No enemy had a fist redder with blood.
What kind of day was this for the Kyrgyz?
Unless the Chinese hero surrendered him to the foe,
The unyielding armored warrior,
The wind could not overtake the Kyrgyz champion.
He attacked an enemy as vast as China.
It was the Kyrgyz hour of action.
Broad-souled hero Kenen,
He split whatever he faced.
The countless host beyond all reckoning,
He ranged through it from end to end.
Without retreating, he thrust his spear.
He was drenched in bloody gore.
Then he remained in his place.
He ranged about, calling for the orphan.
He speared everyone he overtook.
He hammered the glowing iron.
No wind could overtake his passing course.
He made his station known,
And devastated everything in confusion.
Kaanak’s dense host,
He cast into turmoil and destroyed.
Without becoming infirm, they broke through,
And dismounted to contend on foot.
Though orders came by the thousand,
Such was the fist that guarded the pass.
When a dense host of thousands stood,
When the great battle was fought.
The bay horse stood upon the open ridge,
At the boundary no soul could cross,
When he defeated his enemy,
In the hollow of the mountain washed by flood,
God granted him to the Kyrgyz,
When one looked, would the eye catch him?
The day he lay at the foot of the slope,
It was unclear which one he was,
Like one who heard a bitter lament,
The Chinese were many, the people alone,
They were cutting them down and moving on,
The great one known among the Kyrgyz,
Was doing so as he went.
When he met the enemy,
He struck them and passed on,
From humiliation piled upon humiliation,
He split through and passed on.
One man against a thousand men,
He saw them and passed on.
The far side into his hand,
He delivered it and went on.
When he met the wrathful enemy,
He departed over the mountain.
Shattering the Chinese,
He slaughtered them and went on.
Bringing down the great ones in uproar,
He guarded the people’s livestock,
The troubled wealth fell into tumult,
For the white-capped Kyrgyz people,
Shameful oppression became an uproar.
He was a warrior and a lion,
His word was equal among the Kyrgyz,
He began the sword conflict,
His courage tightened with resolve,
Ebegey and Köböy, the two lions,
Parted from the two lions,
His ribs became his courage.
A false vision appeared in the distance.
A shovelful of night fell upon repentance.
A merciless day descended,
Entangled with the fall of night.
Hero Kenen ranged among the enemy.
Such was the wrestler’s courage.
It was the hour when he set his words in order.
He laid hands upon every hardship.
It was the hour when he stood and opposed them.
